question:
Let $f(x)=\sin x+\cos x$ for $x\in[0,2\pi]$.

(a) Determine all critical points lying in $(0,2\pi)$.

(b) Using the sign of the first derivative, find the intervals on which $f$ is increasing and decreasing.

(c) Verify the signs of the derivative by evaluating $f'\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and $f'\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)$.
explanation:
(a)
Differentiation
$$f'(x)=\cos x-\sin x$$
The critical points satisfy
$$\cos x-\sin x=0$$
$$\tan x=1$$
For $x\in(0,2\pi)$, the solutions are
$$x=\frac{\pi}{4}\quad\text{and}\quad x=\frac{5\pi}{4}$$

(b)
Using the identity
$$\cos x-\sin x=\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$$
we examine the sign of $f'(x)$.
On $\left(0,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$, $f'(x)>0$.
On $\left(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)$, $f'(x)<0$.
On $\left(\frac{5\pi}{4},2\pi\right)$, $f'(x)>0$.
Therefore, $f$ is increasing on
$$\left(0,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\cup\left(\frac{5\pi}{4},2\pi\right)$$
and decreasing on
$$\left(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)$$

(c)
At $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$,
$$f'\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\cos\frac{\pi}{2}-\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=0-1=-1<0$$
This agrees with the decreasing behaviour on $\left(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)$.
At $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$,
$$f'\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)=\cos\frac{3\pi}{2}-\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}=0-(-1)=1>0$$
This agrees with the increasing behaviour on $\left(\frac{5\pi}{4},2\pi\right)$.

options.B:
(a) $x=\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{3\pi}{4}$
(b) Increasing between the critical points and decreasing outside
(c) Both derivative values are $-1$
options.C:
(a) $x=\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{7\pi}{4}$
(b) Decreasing on the first and last intervals and increasing in between
(c) Both derivative values are $1$
